title: Second Order Effects of AI: Cheng Lou
talk_summary: Cheng Lou's talk is a speculative design essay about second-order effects of AI (chess improving after Deep Blue, personalized UI, dynamic layouts), not an engineering talk about running agent systems. The one genuinely transferable idea is his contrast between a few expensive smart agents and many cheap dumb nodes aggregated by a smart top-level process.

takeaways.technique: Cheap-node fan-out with a smart aggregator instead of few expensive agents
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues that Smalltalk-style agents that are individually as smart as possible consume so much resource you can only run single digits of them, losing all emergent aggregate behavior; instead use many dumb nodes whose weights/connections are learned and aggregate them under one smart top-level process.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the node are as dumb as they get and when they're dumb and simple you get to have millions of them

takeaways.technique: Match model tier to task granularity, not to task importance
takeaways.what_they_do: Frames the tradeoff as resource intensity per agent determining how many agents you can run at all; being 'too smart at a lower level' forfeits quantity-driven gains.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when each agent takes up enough resource uh you only get to have a single or double digit of them

takeaways.technique: Design-time bulk generation with cheap scoring, not runtime generation
takeaways.what_they_do: Generates thousands of candidate layouts offline at design time with slow algorithms, filters them with a scoring heuristic plus human curation, then at runtime only runs a cheap classifier to pick one.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this is done at design time offline not at runtime so we can use an algorithm that's as slow as we need
takeaways.numbers: thousands of candidates vs a single-digit number of hand-made designs

takeaways.technique: Replace brittle hand-written heuristics with a learned classifier over discretized cases
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues media-query-style hand-coded rules are brittle and less controllable than a simple classifier over a discrete set of curated options, and that the selection problem is classification, not generation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's not an auto regressive problem it's not a diffusion problem it's a simple classification problem
